name: Sidecar
intent: Run a helper process beside each service to handle the shared plumbing, such as logging, retries and TLS, in any language.
scenario: Forty services written in four languages all need the same retry, logging and encryption behaviour when they call each other.
problem: Each service carries its own copy of the networking code, so the same retry rules are written in four languages and drift apart. Changing a rule means rebuilding and redeploying every service.
solution: A Sidecar is a small process deployed next to each service instance, on the same host or in the same pod. The service sends its outbound calls to the sidecar on localhost. The sidecar adds logging, retries, timeouts and encryption, and forwards the call. The service has no networking code, whatever language it is written in, and the sidecar is upgraded on its own.
pain: Retry and logging code is copied into every service
The same behaviour is rewritten in each language
Copies drift: one service retries three times, another never
A policy change means rebuilding and redeploying every service
benefits: Policies are changed and rolled out in the sidecar, without touching the application code
The sidecar has its own life cycle, so it can be upgraded, restarted and monitored separately
whenToUse: Many services, in several languages, need the same cross-cutting behaviour
You want to change network policy without rebuilding applications
A platform team owns the behaviour and application teams should not have to
whenNotToUse: A few services in one language: a shared library is simpler and has no extra hop
Very latency-sensitive paths where an extra local hop matters
When you cannot afford one more process, in memory and in operations, for every instance
pitfalls: Every service now has two things to run, start in order and keep healthy
The extra local hop adds a little latency to every call, and a lot of calls add up
A sidecar crash can take the service's network access with it, so the two must be health-checked together
Large fleets of sidecars multiply memory, CPU and upgrade work, and version mismatches are hard to debug

roles.label: Application
roles.description: The service with the business logic. It talks to the sidecar on localhost.

roles.label: Sidecar
roles.description: The helper process beside it. It adds logging, retries, timeouts and encryption to the app's calls.

roles.label: Remote service
roles.description: Another service on the network that the app wants to call.

quiz.question: A company has 40 services in four languages. Each has its own port of the retry, logging and encryption code, and the ports no longer behave the same. What is the best way to fix this?
options: Choose one language for all new services, and leave the old services as they are
Run a sidecar beside each service that applies one set of rules to all of its calls
Write a long document that describes the rules, and ask each team to follow it
Rewrite the shared code as a library in the most popular of the four languages
quiz.explanation: A sidecar is one implementation that every language can use, because the service just calls localhost. A language choice or a library in one language leaves three languages out, and a document does not stop the copies from drifting.

quiz.question: A team has three services, all written in the same language, and a retry library that works well. A colleague proposes adding a sidecar next to each one. What is the best response?
options: Add the sidecars, since a sidecar is always better than a library for network code
Add them only on the busiest service, so that the cost is paid where it is needed most
Keep the library, because the main benefit, one implementation for many languages, is not needed here
Replace the library with sidecars, but run the sidecars on a different machine for safety
quiz.explanation: The sidecar's strength is a single implementation across languages and teams, at the price of an extra process and hop per instance. With one language and a working library, that price buys nothing. A sidecar on another machine is no longer a sidecar.

quiz.question: A service's sidecar crashes. The service keeps running, but all its outbound calls fail, and the platform team only sees the problem when customers complain. What should the team do?
options: Restart the sidecar and the service as one unit, and health-check them together
Add a second sidecar beside the first, so that one is always running at the same time
Move the retry logic back into the application, so that it does not depend on a sidecar
Increase the sidecar's memory limit, since a sidecar only crashes when it runs out of memory
quiz.explanation: The app and its sidecar share a fate, so they are deployed, started and health-checked as one unit. A service that is up but cannot call out should be marked unhealthy. A second sidecar and more memory do not address that, and moving logic back loses the benefit.
